esdi_renormalization_note: The headline ESDI renormalises the covered sectors (their weights sum to less than 1 because gas and coal are uncovered). The 'uncovered-zero-assumption sensitivity' is the same figure computed under the explicitly FALSE assumption that gas and coal are zero; the gap is the uplift that excluding them adds. It is a sensitivity, not a measured ESDI — unknown stays unknown. Gas carries documented strikes that score zero only for want of a defensible denominator.

transmission_concentration.note: Transmission is an event-burden measure against a saturation constant (8), so it is dominated by the freshest strikes in a thin sector -- currently the Kerch power bridge (Taman) and occupied-Crimea substations, not the wider Russian grid. Read it as theatre-concentrated, not national.

alternative_models.note: A (current): voltage-weighted facility event-burden / global saturation. B: per-region saturation combined breadth-aware, so one theatre cannot consume the proxy. C: breadth (regions) and intensity (worst region) reported SEPARATELY, never one scalar. D: count of distinct currently-impaired facilities (repeat strikes on a node count once). E (remove from headline): see esdi_excluding_transmission on the snapshot. None claims a percent of grid offline.

transmission_sensitivity.note: Transmission is an event-burden against a saturation constant, not a national-grid capacity measure. It is dominated by 1-2 theatres and the headline value roughly halves/doubles as the saturation constant moves between 16 and 4. Published as a sensitivity, not a tuning knob.
transmission_sensitivity.red_team_verdict: RETAINED in the headline as 'Transmission disruption burden' (iteration-7 independent red-team). Model A is the least-bad scalar: it is the only formulation that jointly honours recency, evidence confidence, damage severity and voltage class, is structurally immune to repeat-strike double-counting (a node's strongest live trajectory wins, never the sum), and fits the service-only recovery evidence we actually have (it never needs a reconstitution duration). Alternatives were measured and rejected as a headline: B's breadth-awareness is dormant at current magnitudes; D (distinct-facility count) is the single most misleading number; C (breadth+intensity) is kept only as a supporting display; E (remove entirely) buys just +0.39 of purity while discarding real sourced signal and is the option most exposed to the appearance of tuning occupied Crimea (~45% of the burden) away. The honest fix is LABELLING not surgery: it is a disruption BURDEN of a handful of theatres, never a percent of grid offline, and the ex-transmission counterfactual (esdi_excluding_transmission) is published so the +0.39 it adds is one click away. Its two real wounds — an arbitrary saturation constant (~4x swing) and single-theatre concentration — are disclosed via the sweep, the concentration split and these alternatives.

electric_generation_mw.source: WRI Global Power Plant Database v1.3.0
electric_generation_mw.census_vintage: 2018 (newest Russian commissioning year; no retirement field)
electric_generation_mw.known_bias: over-counts post-2018 retirements, under-counts post-2018 additions

assessed_degradation.note: Assessed degradation counts only capacity a source explicitly quantified. It is deliberately distinct from exposure, which counts capacity at disrupted sites regardless of measured loss.

recovery_stats.note: Recovery is tracked per incident and counted by DISTINCT EPISODE: a multi-day strike counts once. National observed-restoration evidence is n=9. A per-CLASS median appears only where a class has >= 3 independent observed episodes; the pooled cross-class figure is MIXED-INFRASTRUCTURE evidence, not a generic repair time, and is never the headline. 'modelled' scoring means no credible source-reported timing exists; a partial restart (including flow rerouted around a still-damaged node) is recorded but never treated as full reconstitution.

coverage_detail.note: Counts of enumerated events only. A low count may mean genuinely low disruption OR thin open-source reporting for that bucket; this dataset cannot always distinguish the two, and does not pretend to.

graduation_reasons: No matched external denominator exists: the only public total (Gazprom Pererabotka ~110 bcm/y) is operator-scope and spans other federal districts incl. out-of-AOI Amur, so a ratio against it is invalid; no all-Russia or AOI-matched capacity total was found.

Capacities are not internally comparable: the census mixes DESIGN nameplate (Orenburg 45, Astrakhan 12 — actual throughput markedly lower, Astrakhan ~5.4) with actual-throughput figures for others, so the total is not like-for-like.

Non-exhaustive by construction: the largest Russian GPP (Amur, ~42 bcm/y) is correctly out of the AOI; condensate-stabilisation plants (Surgut, Novy Urengoy, Purovsky) are a different function and excluded.
gas_processing.caveat: Within-census share of a non-exhaustive, bottom-up sample of publicly-sourced GPP capacities (bcm/y raw gas) — NOT a national denominator, and NOT like-for-like (it mixes design nameplate with actual throughput). This is a sample, not a percentage of national gas-processing exposure. Experimental: kept out of the headline ESDI, and NOT summed with LNG (MTPA) or gas-transmission (bcm/y pipeline) into any 'Gas' super-score — those are different functions and units.

excluded_condensate_splitters: Surgut Condensate Stabilization Plant (~12 MTPA, Gazprom; condensate, not crude)
Novatek Ust-Luga complex (~9 MTPA; stable gas condensate, not crude)
Astrakhan condensate refining line (~3 MTPA; on the gas-processing census instead)
refinery_reconciliation.note: DENOMINATOR completeness (distinct from event coverage). No major crude refinery is missing: an independent open-source census maps every top-tier Russian refinery to the tracked list. The gap to the full 327 MTPA nameplate is (a) ~24 MTPA of gas-condensate splitters (Surgut CSP, Novatek Ust-Luga, Astrakhan line) that make motor fuels from CONDENSATE not crude and are excluded by the same rule as Tobolsk/ZapSibNeftekhim (6.85 MTPA, the only petrochemical exclusion); and (b) ~29 MTPA because the tracked figures come from one consistent public source (Wikipedia bbl/d, converted) that sits ~10-15% below current nameplate. Consequence for the score: because refining exposure is a capacity SHARE (struck capacity / denominator), a UNIFORM nameplate revaluation -- scaling all tracked plants up together -- leaves the exposure essentially INVARIANT (numerator and denominator scale together); the conservative basis does not systematically bias refining exposure up or down. It mainly affects the absolute MTPA and the completeness ratio against the nameplate reference. (Only a one-sided enlargement of the denominator alone would lower the exposure, which is not what a uniform revaluation does.) The consistent single-source basis is kept deliberately rather than a mixed nameplate basis; a future pass could revalue uniformly. Belarus (Mozyr, Naftan) is correctly outside the Russian denominator.

canonical_linkage.note: Identity/linkage completeness, NOT disruption coverage: how much of the tracked denominator resolves to a struck canonical refinery. Naftan (Belarus) is intentionally outside the Russian denominator.

national.value_text: Reuters (via Moscow Times): as of 20 May 2026, refineries fully halted or significantly reduced after drone strikes totalled >83 Mt/yr of capacity (~238,000 t/day) -- nearly a quarter of Russia's total refining -- accounting for >30% of gasoline output and ~25% of diesel output.
Kyiv Independent (citing the Financial Times): Ukrainian strikes had hit at least 16 of Russia's 38 oil refineries since Aug 2025, pushing Russian diesel exports to their lowest level since 2020.

Moscow Times: Russia extended its gasoline export ban (exporters and producers) through 31 Dec 2025, and barred resellers from selling diesel, marine fuel and other gas oils abroad through end-2025 (direct producers exempt) -- a policy response to strike-driven domestic fuel tightness.

Moscow Times: a Kommersant estimate put the gasoline shortage at 20% (~400,000 t/month). The same article reports as observed fact that two Far East regions and annexed Crimea introduced ration cards for buying gasoline.

Reuters (26 Aug 2025): Ukrainian attacks had disrupted the operation of at least 17% of Russia's oil refining capacity, having recently targeted ten refineries and halting ~1.1 million bbl/d, amid peak seasonal demand.

Moscow Times: on 8 Jul 2026 Deputy PM Novak announced a ban on diesel exports (incl. producers) through 31 Jul 2026 to boost domestic supply after drone strikes. Seaborne diesel/gasoil exports had fallen to ~1.8 Mt in June (down 39% m/m, 46% y/y); early-July diesel exports ran ~187,000 bbl/d vs 535,000 a year earlier.

Bloomberg (13 Aug 2026, via Yahoo Finance): Russia's diesel and gasoil exports fell to just 80,000 bbl/d during 1-7 August 2026, the lowest in several years, versus as much as 1 million bbl/d a year earlier, as drone attacks forced refining capacity offline.

Yahoo (citing Kommersant): AI-95 gasoline on SPIMEX surged above 77,000 rubles/tonne (~$946.6) on 4 Aug 2025, a record, attributed to Ukrainian drone strikes on refineries incl. a 2 Aug strike in Ryazan Oblast.

cur-2026-08-20-taman-500kv.value_text: After the strike on the Taman 500 kV substation, power failed around 01:45 in Simferopol, Sevastopol, Kerch, Feodosia and Yalta; Russian-installed Sevastopol authorities said restrictions were lifted after about 90 minutes, though the grid stayed unstable and some settlements remained without power. No consumer count is given.

cur-orsk-2026-08-11.value_text: Reuters: Orsknefteorgsintez ceased processing on 11 Aug after a fire from the drone attack. Nameplate ~5.76 Mt/yr (~115,200 bbl/d); in 2024 it processed 4.2 Mt of crude. (Moscow Times separately cites 6.6 Mt/yr; conflict preserved.)

Moscow Times: with the refinery fully shut, the Orenburg governor said the region would rely on fuel trucked in, and that 80% of the region's 287 filling stations were operational, priority to emergency vehicles.

Moscow Times: the Orenburg governor said repairs could take up to six months because shrapnel damaged key infrastructure hard to replace under Western sanctions. A projection, not an observed restart.

gazprom-neftekhim-salavat:2026-07-13.value_text: Meduza (industry data): the 14 July overnight strike disabled both primary crude distillation units at Salavat -- CDU-6 (17,140 t/day) and CDU-4 (11,430 t/day) -- taking the complex offline. The plant was ~2.7% of Russia's total refining throughput in 2024.

cur-2026-06-24-orenburg-gpp.value_text: World Oil: after the 24 June strike forced the Orenburg GPP to suspend intake of Karachaganak raw gas, output at Kazakhstan's Karachaganak field was cut by more than a quarter -- 34,000 t/day normally to 25,000 t/day (~180,000 bbl/d). Field oil and gas output are linked. (Interfax gives different figures; both preserved.)

Interfax (citing KazMunayGas): Karachaganak output was cut by 9,000 t/day on 26 June -- to ~28,000 from ~31,000 -- after the Orenburg plant incident, and as of 30 June was not yet fully restored. (Baseline differs from World Oil; both reported unmerged.)

cur-2025-02-03-astrakhan-gpp.value_text: Reuters (via Ukrinform): the early-Feb 2025 strike halted fuel output at Gazprom's Astrakhan GPP; the damaged gas-condensate unit has ~3 Mt/yr capacity, and industry sources said it might only resume in weeks or months. (Value is the affected unit's annual capacity; the halt is the observed effect.)

perm-refinery:2026-04-29.value_text: Reuters (via RBC-Ukraine): the CDU-4 (AVT-4) primary unit at LUKOIL's Perm refinery was out from 30 April after the 29 April strike/fire; a 7 May strike shut three more primary units and completely halted processing. The refinery ran ~12.6 Mt of crude in 2024 (~250,000 bbl/d).

syzran-refinery:2026-04-18.value_text: Hydrocarbon Processing (citing Reuters/industry): Rosneft's Syzran refinery halted processing after the 18 April attack, shutting primary unit CDU-6, which is >70% of plant capacity. Capacity 8.5 Mt/yr (~170,000 bbl/d).

volgograd-refinery:2026-06-01.value_text: Militarnyi: LUKOIL's Volgograd refinery suspended operations after the strike (this source dates it to the night of 29 May 2026 -- 2-3 days before the incident's 2026-06-01 label; likely the same event). Primary distillation unit No. 1 (~40% of capacity) stopped, as did units 5 and 6. Capacity 14.8 Mt/yr of products (~300,000 bbl/d).

kirishi-refinery-kinef:2026-05-05.value_text: Moscow Times (Reuters/industry): Kirishi (KINEF) halted around 5 May 2026 after drones damaged three of its four crude distillation units plus secondary units; the plant handled ~7% of Russia's refining, ~350,000 bbl/d. Repair timeline unclear.

kirishi-refinery-kinef:2025-10-04.value_text: Ukrinform (industry data): the 4 Oct 2025 strike knocked out Kirishi's CDU-6 primary unit -- 8 Mt/yr (~160,000 bbl/d), ~40% of the refinery's capacity; a mid-September strike had damaged another unit. Plant processed 17.5 Mt in 2024, 6.6% of Russia's volume.

ryazan-refinery:2025-01-24.value_text: Reuters (via Yahoo): after the 24 Jan 2025 strike Ryazan stopped oil processing and suspended all rail fuel loadings (a loading track and hydrotreater damaged); ~17 Mt/yr capacity, nearly 5% of Russia's refining in 2024.

ryazan-refinery:2026-05-15.value_text: Ukrinform (Reuters; units per Ukraine's General Staff): Ryazan suspended operations after the 15 May 2026 strike, which damaged the AVT-3, AVT-4 and AT-6 units and a diesel hydrotreater. Processed 13.1 Mt in 2024, ~5% of Russia's capacity.

novokuibyshevsk-refinery:2026-06-02.value_text: Ukrainska Pravda (22 Aug 2026): a June 2026 drone attack on Rosneft's Novokuibyshevsk refinery (design ~8.8 Mt/yr) caused a temporary crude-processing suspension; an earlier April strike had shut units AVT-11 and AVT-9. (Reporting dates the June strike to 10 June vs the dataset's 2 June label; likely the same episode.)

cur-novoshakhtinsk-2026-08-25.value_text: Moscow Times (Rostov region authorities): the Novoshakhtinsk refinery sustained damage and temporarily suspended processing after the 25 Aug 2026 drone attack. No throughput figure given.

cur-crimea-kerch-tpp-2026-06-23.value_text: Kyiv Independent (Russian occupation spokesperson Kryuchkov): after the 23 Jun 2026 strikes (Kerch TPP fuel reservoirs, Simferopol gas distribution, West Crimea 330/110 kV substation), ~half the peninsula was left without electricity and rolling load-shedding introduced. A proxy PROPORTION claim, NOT a consumer/household count.
